parts.title: The art of bargaining
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
My first trip to a market abroad was a lesson I will never forget. I was in Morocco, and I saw a beautiful brass lamp. The seller said, "Fifty euros, my friend." That seemed a fair price, so I put my hand in my pocket.

Suddenly, a local man standing nearby said quietly, "Never accept the first price. Offer half." I was embarrassed, but I tried. "Twenty-five," I said. The seller looked shocked and put his hand on his heart. "My family will go hungry!" he said. I smiled. The man next to me whispered that it was part of the game.

We went back and forth for ten minutes. The seller dropped his price to forty, then thirty-five, while I increased mine to thirty. In the end, we agreed on thirty-two euros and shook hands. Then he gave me a glass of mint tea, and we talked about football for half an hour.

Later, my guide told me that the real price was probably twenty. I did not mind. I had learned something, made a new friend and bought a lamp that still stands in my living room.

questions.prompt: What was the first price?
questions.explanation: The seller asked fifty euros.

questions.prompt: What did the local man advise?
questions.explanation: He said never accept the first price and offer half.

questions.prompt: How did the seller react to the offer?
questions.explanation: He acted shocked and said his family would go hungry, but it was part of the game.

questions.prompt: What happened after they agreed?
questions.explanation: He gave her mint tea, and they talked about football.

questions.prompt: How did the writer feel at the end?
questions.explanation: She did not mind; she had learned something and made a friend.

parts.title: The oldest markets in the world
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Markets are older than shops. [1] Long before there were coins, people met in open places to swap food, tools and cloth.

In ancient cities, markets were often the busiest and loudest place in town. [2] Crowds of people came from the villages to sell their goods and to hear the news.

In the Middle Ages, European towns held weekly market days. [3] The law said that nobody was allowed to sell goods outside the market square.

Some markets became famous across the world. [4] The Grand Bazaar in Istanbul has over four thousand shops, and some of them have been owned by the same family for centuries.

Today, many people buy online, but markets are still popular. [5] They offer something that a website cannot: a chance to touch, smell and taste before you buy.
sentences: Each town had its own rules.
Many people say they prefer the lively atmosphere.
Nobody knows when the first one began.
People like to meet and talk as well as shop.
Millions of visitors go to see them every year.

gaps.explanation: Nobody knows when the first market began; the next sentence says people met before coins.
People liked to meet and talk; the next sentence says crowds came from the villages.
Each town had its own rules; the next sentence says nobody could sell outside the square.
Millions of visitors go to see them; the next sentence gives the Grand Bazaar as an example.
Many people prefer the lively atmosphere; the next sentence says markets offer touch, smell and taste.

parts.title: Buying second-hand
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Buying second-hand clothes or furniture is a good way to save money and to help the planet. When you buy something that someone else has used, you give it [1] new life and reduce waste. Markets and charity shops are great places to look. Always check the item carefully [2] you pay for it. Look for holes, stains or broken parts. Smell it, too, because bad smells are hard to remove. Do not be afraid to ask for a lower price, as sellers [3] expect it. If the object is electrical, ask the seller to show you that it works. For clothes, try them on if you can, because sizes are different in every country. [4] you cannot try them on, measure them with a tape. Finally, wash everything carefully when you get home. With a little patience, you can find [5] fantastic bargains, and you will never again want to pay full price [6] a new item.

gaps.explanation: Give something a new life: indefinite article.
Check before you pay: sequence of actions.
If you cannot try them on: condition.
Find some fantastic bargains: plural quantity.

parts.title: A message from the market manager
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: manager
turns.text: Good morning, traders and visitors. This is Enoch, the market manager, with some news. As of next month, the market will open an hour earlier, at seven in the morning. We will also add a new day, Thursday, so we will be open four days a week. The new food court will be in the south corner, near the car park, and will have twelve stalls. In the middle of the square, we are building a small stage, where musicians will perform at weekends. All stall owners must pay an extra five pounds for the electricity. We are also introducing a new rule about plastic: from the first of May, no plastic bags will be allowed. Customers should bring their own bags or buy a cloth bag from the information stand for one pound. Thank you for your help.

gaps.prompt: The market will open at ___ in the morning
gaps.explanation: He says the market will open at seven.
He says they will add Thursday.

gaps.prompt: The food court will have ___ stalls
gaps.explanation: He says it will have twelve stalls.

gaps.prompt: Musicians will play on a ___ in the square
gaps.explanation: He says a small stage is being built.

gaps.prompt: Stall owners must pay ___ pounds extra
gaps.explanation: He says an extra five pounds for the electricity.
He says a cloth bag is one pound.

parts.title: An interview with a market trader
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Pike, you have sold vegetables at this market for thirty years. What do you love about it?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: The people. I know all my customers by name, and I know what they like. Mrs Brown always wants the smallest potatoes.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Is it a hard life?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Very. I get up at three in the morning to buy fresh produce at the wholesale market. By six, my stall must be ready.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you do in bad weather?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: We stay. Rain, wind or snow, customers still need their vegetables. I wear three jumpers and a hat.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: How has the business changed?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Supermarkets are the main competition. But people say that my carrots taste better, and I think they are right.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What advice would you give to a young trader?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Be honest, smile and never sell anything you would not eat yourself.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Will you retire soon?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: My daughter wants to take over the stall, so I think I can stop in a few years. But I will visit every Saturday.

questions.explanation: He says to be honest, smile and sell only what you would eat.
